artiest/debbie-harry.text:
Debbie Harry is an American singer, songwriter and actress, best known as the lead singer of Blondie. She was born in Miami in 1945 and grew up in Hawthorne, New Jersey. Before her breakthrough she worked as a dancer, a Playboy Bunny and a secretary, including a spell at the BBC in New York. In the late 1960s she was a backing singer in the folk rock group The Wind in the Willows, and in 1973 she joined The Stillettoes, where she met Chris Stein. In 1974 the two of them formed Blondie in New York.

Blondie released their debut album in 1976. With Parallel Lines in 1978 the group became known worldwide. Four of the band's songs reached number one on the US Hot 100 between 1979 and 1981. With her bleached hair, daring clothes and tough image, Harry became a punk icon and the face of new wave. Her image was so closely tied to the group that many people thought Blondie was her own name. In 1981 her first solo album, KooKoo, followed, and later Rockbird in 1986 and Debravation in 1993. She also acted in films, such as David Cronenberg's Videodrome from 1983. Blondie reunited in the late 1990s and released No Exit, among other albums.

Harry thus became one of the faces of new wave and showed how a female singer could embody a band.
artiest/debbie-harry.listen: Listen to Heart of Glass from Parallel Lines. Notice how the beat and the vocals together sound cool and danceable, and how little this resembles classic punk.

artiest/dee-snider.text:
Dee Snider is an American singer and radio and television personality, best known as the singer and songwriter of the heavy metal band Twisted Sister. He was born in 1955 in Astoria, a neighbourhood of Queens, New York. In 1976 he joined Twisted Sister and wrote almost all of their material. The group first built up a following mainly in Great Britain.

Their debut album Under the Blade appeared in 1982, and You Can't Stop Rock 'n' Roll a year later. Their greatest success was the third album, Stay Hungry, from 1984, with the hits We're Not Gonna Take It and I Wanna Rock. We're Not Gonna Take It reached number two in the British charts and number 21 on the US Hot 100. Come Out and Play followed in 1985. That same year Snider became known to a wider audience when he testified before the US Senate against the Parents Music Resource Center, which wanted to put warning labels on records with offensive lyrics. Later he made solo records, such as Never Let the Bastards Wear You Down in 2000 and For the Love of Metal in 2018, and worked in radio and television.

Snider stands for the theatrical side of 1980s metal, with shouted choruses, make-up and a rebellious image. His appearance before the Senate was regarded as a famous moment in the fight for freedom in popular music.
artiest/dee-snider.listen: Listen to We're Not Gonna Take It and pay attention to the chorus. Why is it so easy to sing along with a whole hall?

artiest/deep-purple.text:
Deep Purple was formed in London in 1968. In the best-known line-up, known as Mark II, the band consisted of singer Ian Gillan, guitarist Ritchie Blackmore, bassist Roger Glover, organist Jon Lord and drummer Ian Paice. Together with Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath, Deep Purple is regarded as a founder of hard rock and heavy metal; the three British bands were nicknamed the 'unholy trinity'.

Their first hit was Hush (1968), a cover of a Joe South song, which reached number 4 in America. With In Rock (1970) the band chose a much heavier sound. In Child in Time Gillan sings high up in his falsetto. Jon Lord played his Hammond organ through Marshall amplifiers, so that it sounded just as loud and distorted as Blackmore's guitar. In December 1971 the band wanted to record an album in Montreux, but during a concert by Frank Zappa the casino burned down after someone fired a flare gun. The band turned that story into Smoke on the Water, for the album Machine Head (1972), which was recorded in the corridors of a hotel. Released as a single, the song reached number 4 in America in 1973.

The live album Made in Japan (1972) captured the band at the peak of their form. In 1975 the Guinness Book of Records named Deep Purple the loudest band in the world, after a concert at London's Rainbow Theatre. In 1976 the group broke up; in 1984 Mark II got back together. In 2016 Deep Purple was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Jon Lord died in 2012.
artiest/deep-purple.listen: Smoke on the Water (1972): notice the riff at the start. Blackmore plays a four-note melody in G minor, each time on two strings at once, a fourth apart. Without a third, the sound stays clear, even with heavy distortion.

artiest/def-p.text:
Def P's real name is Pascal Griffioen. He was born in Amsterdam in 1969 and grew up in Osdorp. At sixteen he took the name Def P and began writing rap lyrics. During a holiday in the United States in 1988 he played people some hip hop from the Netherlands and was laughed at because the Dutch were imitating Americans. That spurred him on to rap in Dutch.

In 1989, together with his cousin DJ IJsblok and his friends Seda and King Arthur, he founded the Osdorp Posse. A year later the song Moordenaar appeared. Seda made the beats with converted game consoles. In 1992 the group signed to Djax, the Eindhoven label of Saskia Slegers. The Osdorp Posse rapped in broad Amsterdam dialect about life as it was, raw and without any concern for polite language. In doing so the group laid the foundations of Dutch hip hop (nederhop). In 1998 the group started its own label, RAMP, and in 2009 the Osdorp Posse came to an end, after a farewell concert at the Melkweg.

Alongside the group Def P made solo albums, such as Cryptokilostijl and Pascal-rascal, and records with the Beatbusters. For years he presented a radio programme on Kink FM, made radio plays and theatre, wrote columns and drew a graphic novel. Increasingly he is turning to painting. He shows that rap in Dutch does not have to be an imitation of American rap.
artiest/def-p.listen: Listen to a track by the Osdorp Posse, such as Moordenaar. Notice the language: Def P raps in broad Amsterdam dialect, hard and direct, over a bare, heavy beat.

artiest/deftones.text:
Deftones are an American alternative metal band from Sacramento, California, who began in 1988. Singer Chino Moreno, guitarist Stephen Carpenter and drummer Abe Cunningham were childhood friends who went to school together and were part of the city's skateboarding scene. Bassist Chi Cheng joined the group in 1990, and keyboard player and turntablist Frank Delgado in 1999. Carpenter came up with the name by combining the hip hop word def with the suffix tones, which is also a pun on tone-deaf.

After signing with Maverick Records, the debut Adrenaline appeared in 1995. The band built up a loyal fan base by touring a great deal and through word of mouth. The second album, Around the Fur, from 1997, went platinum in the United States, and White Pony, from 2000, showed a shift from a more aggressive to a more experimental sound. In 2008 Cheng was involved in a car accident, after which he died in 2013. Sergio Vega of Quicksand took his place. Since 2010 Diamond Eyes, Koi No Yokan, Gore, Ohms and Private Music have appeared.

Moreno came from hardcore punk, post-punk and new wave, such as Bad Brains, Depeche Mode and The Cure, while Carpenter loved thrash metal. You can hear that mixture in the music: heavy guitars are combined with an atmospheric mood. As a result Deftones became one of the best-known bands of 1990s alternative metal.
artiest/deftones.listen: Listen to My Own Summer (Shove It) and notice the contrast between the heavy guitar riff and Chino Moreno's voice, which can go from restrained to screaming. What atmosphere does this create?

artiest/del-the-funky-homosapien.text:
Del the Funky Homosapien is the stage name of Teren Delvon Jones, an American rapper from Oakland, California, born in 1972. He is a cousin of the West Coast rapper Ice Cube and began his career writing lyrics for Da Lench Mob, Ice Cube's group. In 1991, with Ice Cube's help, he released his first solo album, I Wish My Brother George Was Here, when he was nineteen.

With No Need for Alarm in 1993 the Oakland collective Hieroglyphics came to attention, which included Souls of Mischief, Casual, Pep Love, Del and the producer Domino. The group drew attention both to the regional sound of Oakland and to the freestyle rap of the golden age of the 1990s. After a break of several years Del lost his contract with Elektra, and with his group he founded his own label, Hieroglyphics Imperium Recordings. In 2000 Both Sides of the Brain followed, and he worked on Deltron 3030 with Dan the Automator and Kid Koala. He was also a guest rapper on Gorillaz's first album in 2001, including on Clint Eastwood. Later he released Eleventh Hour in 2008, among other records, and put work online for free.

Del shows how the independent hip hop of Oakland was able to develop free of the major labels.
artiest/del-the-funky-homosapien.listen: Listen to his rap on Clint Eastwood by Gorillaz. Notice how relaxed his voice sounds and how he plays rhythmically with words.

artiest/delfeayo-marsalis.text:
Delfeayo Marsalis is an American jazz trombonist, producer and teacher. He was born in New Orleans in 1965, the son of the pianist and music professor Ellis Marsalis Jr. His brothers Wynton, Branford and Jason Marsalis are a trumpeter, a saxophonist and a drummer, and in 2011 the whole family received the NEA Jazz Masters Award. He studied at the Berklee College of Music and in 2004 earned a master's degree in jazz trombone at the University of Louisville.

Delfeayo recorded eight albums of his own, including Pontius Pilate's Decision in 1992, Musashi in 1997, Sweet Thunder in 2011 and The Last Southern Gentlemen in 2014. He is best known as a producer of acoustic jazz records. Together with the sound engineer Patrick Smith he came up with a phrase about getting more wood sound from the bass without plugging the bass in directly. That phrase first appeared on his brother Branford's album Renaissance from 1987, and from then on it served as a benchmark for the recording quality of a great deal of acoustic jazz from the late 1980s onwards. In 2000 he founded the Uptown Music Theatre in New Orleans, which has trained more than three hundred young people.

In this way Marsalis contributes to the sound of modern acoustic jazz not only as a trombonist but above all as a producer, and he continues the musical family tradition of New Orleans.
artiest/delfeayo-marsalis.listen: Listen to a track from Sweet Thunder and notice the tone of the trombone. Is it warm or sharp, and how does it relate to the rest of the band?

artiest/delia-derbyshire.text: Delia Derbyshire, from Coventry, studied mathematics and music at Cambridge. From 1962 she worked at the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, the broadcaster's electronic studio. In 1963 she created there the sound of Ron Grainer's Doctor Who theme. There was no synthesizer yet: she recorded single tones from oscillators and noise on tape, sped them up and slowed them down, and spliced them together piece by piece. Grainer was so impressed that he wanted to credit her as co-composer, but the BBC would not allow it. She also made music for documentaries and radio, such as Blue Veils and Golden Sands (1968).
artiest/delia-derbyshire.listen: Notice how the bass line and the floating melody are made from recorded and cut-up sounds, not from played instruments.

artiest/delia-derbyshire-bbc-radiophonic.text:
The BBC Radiophonic Workshop was a sound department of the BBC, founded in 1958 to create special sounds and new music for radio and later television. Daphne Oram set it up in 1957 with Desmond Briscoe, and the workshop was based in the Maida Vale Studios in London. At first the group mainly made effects for experimental radio plays, including for the science fiction serial Quatermass and the Pit and for The Goon Show. From the early 1960s, signature tunes for television followed. In 1998 the Workshop closed.

Delia Derbyshire was one of its members, alongside Daphne Oram, David Cain, John Baker and Paddy Kingsland, among others. In 1963 the composer Ron Grainer asked the Workshop for the theme tune for the new series Doctor Who. He had written a score with directions such as sweeps, swoops, wind clouds and wind bubbles, and Derbyshire turned that into a piece of electronic music that has become one of the best-known television themes.

The music of the Workshop is experimental electronic music, made with equipment that was among the most advanced in the country at the time. The group's work points ahead to electronic pop music, even though it was intended for the BBC. Derbyshire stands for a time when electronic sounds were still made and edited by hand, and her work is a source of inspiration for later artists.
artiest/delia-derbyshire-bbc-radiophonic.listen: Listen to Blue Veils and Golden Sands and notice the unusual, electronic sounds that do not seem to come from an ordinary instrument. What atmosphere do they create, and which sounds stay with you?

artiest/demis-roussos.text:
Demis Roussos was a Greek singer who was born in 1946 in Alexandria, Egypt, into a Greek family. As a child he sang in the city's Byzantine church choir and came into contact with jazz, Arabic music and Greek Orthodox music. After the Suez Crisis of 1956 the family moved to Greece. There he played in bands, including the Idols, where he met Vangelis and Loukas Sideras, his later bandmates in Aphrodite's Child.

With that progressive rock group he broke through internationally. His operatic style of singing contributed to the success of their last album, 666, based on passages from the Book of Revelation and later a cult classic. In 1971 Roussos began a solo career with We Shall Dance, which reached the top ten in the Netherlands and Belgium. The peak came in the mid-1970s, with hit albums and singles such as Forever and Ever, My Friend the Wind and Happy to Be on an Island in the Sun, his first hit in Great Britain. In the 1980s he remained successful mainly in France, with Quand je t'aime, among other songs. With Vangelis he later made the album Magic and Race to the End, a version of Chariots of Fire.

Roussos sold more than sixty million albums and, with his kaftans, became a striking figure in European pop.
artiest/demis-roussos.listen: Listen to Forever and Ever and notice his voice. Do you hear something of an operatic voice in this pop song?

artiest/dennis-bovell.text:
Dennis Bovell is a reggae guitarist, bassist and producer who was born in Barbados in 1953 and moved to South London in 1965. There he became devoted to Jamaican culture, above all to dub music, and set up his own sound system, Jah Sufferer. That led to trouble with the police, and he spent six months on remand before being released on appeal. He played in a progressive rock group that later became the British reggae band Matumbi, and recorded dub reggae himself under his own name.

He worked as an engineer at Dip Records, the forerunner of the label Lovers Rock, and played a key role in the early years of the lovers rock genre. His best-known production is Silly Games by Janet Kay, in which he tried to combine disco rhythms with reggae. As a producer he worked with a wide range of artists, including Creation Rebel, I-Roy, the Thompson Twins, Bananarama, The Pop Group, Fela Kuti, The Slits, Orange Juice and Madness. For the greater part of his career he worked with the poet Linton Kwesi Johnson. In 1980 he wrote the music for the film Babylon. In 2020 he had a cameo in Lovers Rock, a film in Steve McQueen's Small Axe series, in which Silly Games features prominently. In 2021 he was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire.

Bovell shows how Caribbean music in London acquired a British sound of its own, and that as a producer he also helped pop bands such as The Pop Group and The Slits.
artiest/dennis-bovell.listen: Listen to Silly Games by Janet Kay. Notice how reggae and disco rhythm run into each other.

artiest/dennis-cahill.text:
Dennis Cahill was an American guitarist who specialised in traditional Irish music. He was born in Chicago in 1954, the son of parents from County Kerry in Ireland. He began playing the guitar at the age of nine and later studied at the Chicago Musical College. He played in Chicago's Irish folk scene.

In the late 1980s, with the Irish fiddler Martin Hayes, he formed the band Midnight Court, which combined traditional music with rock and roll. Cahill played a Fender Telecaster and Hayes an electric fiddle. The band existed from 1989 to 1992. After that the two continued to work together as a duo. In 1999 a reviewer for the New York Times wrote that Hayes and Cahill strip old reels and jigs back to their essence, with room between the notes for flageolets and whispered blue notes, comparable to Steve Reich or Miles Davis's Sketches of Spain. They toured extensively and released albums, such as The Lonesome Touch in 1997 and Welcome Here Again in 2008. Cahill died in 2022.

The duo showed that traditional Irish music can also sound calm and sparing, with plenty of space between the notes.
artiest/dennis-cahill.listen: Listen to a track from The Lonesome Touch. Notice how guitar and fiddle play together and how much space is left between the notes.

artiest/dennis-russell-davies.text:
Dennis Russell Davies is an American conductor and pianist. He was born in 1944 and studied piano and conducting at the Juilliard School, where he earned his doctorate. He was music director of the Saint Paul Chamber Orchestra from 1972 to 1980. In 1977, with the composer Francis Thorne, he founded the American Composers Orchestra. In 1980 he moved to Stuttgart, where until 1987 he was general music director of the Baden-Württemberg opera. There he conducted the premieres of two operas by Philip Glass, in productions with distinctive staging. Later he led the Brno Philharmonic and the MDR Symphony Orchestra in Leipzig, among others.

Davies is best known as an interpreter of living composers. He worked with Philip Glass, Arvo Pärt, John Cage, Lou Harrison and Alan Hovhaness, and performed and recorded a great deal of their work, such as Glass's opera Akhnaten in 1987 and Pärt's Fratres. Glass dedicated his Fifth Symphony to him. For his recording of Copland's Appalachian Spring with the Saint Paul Chamber Orchestra he received a Grammy in 1979. He also worked for a long time with the jazz pianist Keith Jarrett, whom he conducted in concerts of Mozart, Lou Harrison and Alan Hovhaness.

Davies built a bridge between the classical tradition and the music of his own time.
artiest/dennis-russell-davies.listen: Listen to Arvo Pärt's Fratres in one of his recordings. Notice how simple the material is.

artiest/denniz-pop.text:
Denniz PoP's real name was Dag Krister Volle. He was born in 1963 in Tullinge, near Stockholm, the son of Norwegian immigrants. He took his stage name from the comic strip Dennis the Menace, with pop added. In the 1980s he became a DJ and began making remixes and records of his own. In 1986, with others, he founded SweMix, a collective of DJs that made remixes. In 1988 he released Gimme Some Mo' (Bass on Me) under his own name.

His first success as a producer was Hello Afrika by Dr. Alban, from 1990. The two knew each other from playing in clubs. In 1992, with the investor Tom Talomaa, he opened Cheiron Studios in Stockholm, and a year later he brought in Max Martin. From Cheiron he wrote and produced for Ace of Base, Leila K, E-Type, Robyn, the Backstreet Boys, *NSYNC and Britney Spears. At first that was Eurodance, later glossy teen pop: tightly produced, with clear melodies and choruses that stick immediately.

In 1997 he was diagnosed with stomach cancer, and in August 1998 he died, aged 35. Britney Spears dedicated an award to him. Cheiron became the beginning of a wave of Swedish producers and songwriters who shaped global pop in the 1990s and after, with Max Martin the best known. Since 2013 the Denniz Pop Awards have existed for Scandinavian creators.
artiest/denniz-pop.listen: Listen to All That She Wants by Ace of Base. Notice the slow reggae beat, the cool synthesizers and the chorus that sticks like a slogan: the sound with which the Swedish hit factory began.

artiest/denny-laine.text:
Denny Laine, born Brian Frederick Hines, was an English musician who co-founded two major rock groups: The Moody Blues and Paul McCartney and Wings. He was born in Birmingham in 1944 and picked up the guitar as a boy, inspired by the jazz guitarist Django Reinhardt. In 1964 he joined Ray Thomas and Mike Pinder, who were forming a new band that soon came to be called The Moody Blues. He sang lead on their first big hit, a version of Go Now by Bessie Banks.

In December 1966 he left the group and formed the Electric String Band, with electrically amplified strings. After that he played in the band Balls and in Ginger Baker's Air Force, among others, and recorded two singles solo for the label Deram. In 1971 he became a member of Wings, Paul McCartney's band, of which he was the only constant besides McCartney until 1981. He played guitar, bass and keyboards there and sang backing vocals and sometimes lead. Together with McCartney he wrote the song Mull of Kintyre from 1977. Later he recorded Ahh... Laine! in 1974 and Holly Days in 1977, among others.

Laine shows how one musician formed a bridge between the British beat bands of the early 1960s and the pop music of the 1970s.
artiest/denny-laine.listen: Listen to Go Now by The Moody Blues. Notice Laine's singing, the lead vocal on this first big hit by the group.

artiest/depeche-mode.text:
Depeche Mode is an English electronic band from Basildon in Essex, formed in 1980. Vince Clarke, Andy Fletcher and Martin Gore first played together as Composition of Sound. Later in 1980 singer Dave Gahan joined, after Clarke had heard him sing Heroes by David Bowie. Gahan chose the new name, after a French fashion magazine. Because synthesizers were becoming affordable, the group opted for synth-pop. Daniel Miller of the label Mute heard them play and released their first single.

The debut album Speak & Spell from 1981, with the cheerful hit Just Can't Get Enough, was mainly Clarke's work. At the end of 1981 he left and started Yazoo and later Erasure. Martin Gore became the main songwriter, and with Alan Wilder joining, the sound became heavier and darker. Albums such as Some Great Reward, with People Are People, Black Celebration and Music for the Masses made Depeche Mode one of the most popular alternative bands of the 1980s. In 1990 came Violator, with Enjoy the Silence.

Depeche Mode showed that electronic pop music could be sombre, sensual and grand, with dark lyrics by Gore and Gahan's deep voice. Later guitars were added too. Wilder left in 1995, Fletcher died in 2022, and Gahan and Gore carried on together. The band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2020.
artiest/depeche-mode.listen: Listen first to Just Can't Get Enough and then to Enjoy the Silence. Notice the difference: first light, bouncing synthesizers, later a dark, slow atmosphere with Dave Gahan's deep voice.

artiest/derek-bailey.text: The guitarist Derek Bailey, from Sheffield, worked for years as a musician in dance bands, in clubs and for television. From the 1960s he gave that up and in London developed a radically free way of playing, in which there is no longer any melody, chord changes or fixed metre. He used large leaps, harmonics and sounds from the strings. In 1970, with Evan Parker and Tony Oxley, he founded the label Incus, and from 1976 he organised Company, shifting groups of improvisers. His book Improvisation (1980) is a standard work. On Ballads (2002) he plays well-known songs after all, in his own way.
artiest/derek-bailey.listen: Hear the guitar without chords or melody: separate sounds that follow a logic of their own.

artiest/derrick-may.text:
Derrick May is an American electronic musician, born in 1963 in Detroit. He grew up as an only child with his mother. At high school in Belleville, a suburb of Detroit, he became friends with Juan Atkins and Kevin Saunderson. Atkins taught the other two to DJ, and together they formed Deep Space Soundworks, to play their favourite music at parties. They loved Kraftwerk and disco, and listened to the Detroit radio DJ The Electrifying Mojo. Later they came to be called the Belleville Three.

In 1986 May founded the label Transmat. Under the name Rhythim Is Rhythim he released Nude Photo in 1987, and a year later Strings of Life. That track, with fast piano chords and string sounds but no bass line, became one of the classics of techno. Frankie Knuckles gave it that name when he played an early version in Chicago. In England it took off during the house boom of 1987 and 1988.

May calls his music Hi-Tek Soul, and once described it as George Clinton meeting Kraftwerk in an elevator. His music combines tight electronic rhythms with warmth and feeling. After the 1980s he released little new music, but he kept DJing around the world and helped younger artists such as Carl Craig. He has been called the Miles Davis of techno. Since 2020 he has been accused of sexual abuse by several women, which he denies.
artiest/derrick-may.listen: Listen to Strings of Life by Rhythim Is Rhythim. Notice the fast piano chords and the string sounds above the driving beat, and note that there is almost no bass line.

artiest/derrick-morgan.text:
Derrick Morgan is a Jamaican singer, born in 1940, and one of the great names of ska and early reggae. In 1957 he won the talent contest Vere Johns Opportunity Hour in Kingston with imitations of Little Richard. After that he toured the island with the comic duo Bim and Bam. In 1959 he recorded for the first time, for Duke Reid and his label Treasure Isle, with the shuffle boogie number Lover Boy and Oh My.

In 1960 he was the only artist ever to occupy the first seven places in the Jamaican charts at the same time, with songs such as Don't Call Me Daddy and In My Heart. A year later came his biggest hit, Housewives' Choice, produced by Leslie Kong. From it grew a rivalry with Prince Buster, who accused Morgan of stealing his ideas and answered with Blackhead Chiney Man. Morgan responded with Blazing Fire. In 1962 he had a great success with Forward March, a song about Jamaican independence. When ska turned into rocksteady he kept making records, such as the rude boy numbers Tougher Than Tough and Conquering Ruler, and his version of Ben E. King's Seven Letters, produced by Bunny Lee. Later he was still active in the 1970s and wrote songs for other artists that won the Festival Song Contest.

Morgan played in the same world as Desmond Dekker, Bob Marley and Jimmy Cliff and showed how Jamaican pop music developed further in the 1960s, from ska to rocksteady and skinhead reggae. In 2017 he was still appearing at a ska festival in the United States.
artiest/derrick-morgan.listen: Listen to Forward March or Seven Letters. Notice the cheerful offbeat of the ska or the calmer tempo of the rocksteady.

artiest/desmond-child.text:
Desmond Child, born John Charles Barrett, is an American songwriter and producer. He was born in Miami in 1953. His mother was the Cuban songwriter Elena Casals. Only at the age of eighteen did he discover that his biological father was a Hungarian baron. In 1975 he started the pop rock band Desmond Child & Rouge, with three female singers. That band made two well-received but poorly selling albums and stopped in 1980.

After that Child became mainly a writer for others. He co-wrote I Was Made for Lovin' You for Kiss, You Give Love a Bad Name and Livin' on a Prayer for Bon Jovi, Dude (Looks Like a Lady) and Crazy for Aerosmith, Poison for Alice Cooper and Livin' la Vida Loca for Ricky Martin. His strength lies in big, singalong choruses that give rock bands a poppy edge. In 1991 he had a minor hit of his own with Love on a Rooftop.

Child is a good example of an outside writer: he worked with a band on a song so that it became a hit. In the rock of the 1980s in particular, in which bands liked to present themselves as a distinctive group, he often stood invisibly behind the biggest successes. He also worked with Cher, Bonnie Tyler, Roxette and Kelly Clarkson. In 2008 he was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame.
artiest/desmond-child.listen: Listen to Livin' on a Prayer by Bon Jovi. Notice how the song builds up to the chorus and how that chorus, with the whole band singing along, is made so that a stadium can roar it back.

artiest/desmond-dekker.text:
Desmond Dekker's real name was Desmond Adolphus Dacres. He was born in 1941 in Kingston, Jamaica, and as a child went to church with his grandmother and aunt, where he loved singing hymns. He trained as a tailor and then became a welder. His colleagues heard him singing while he worked and urged him to make music. In 1961 he got a contract with Leslie Kong. He also brought his fellow welder Bob Marley to Kong's attention, and Kong made his first records.

In 1963 he had his first Jamaican hit with Honour Your Mother and Father, and with King of Ska he became one of the island's biggest stars. With his backing group The Aces he made ska and rocksteady. With 007 (Shanty Town) from 1967 he sang about the rude boys, the youths from the ghettos of Kingston. That song also became popular in England with the mods.

In 1969 Israelites reached number 1 in England and the top ten in America, one of the first international reggae hits. In England young working-class people, including the early skinheads, found this music in their own way. It Mek and You Can Get It If You Really Want also became hits. Around 1980 he recorded new versions for Stiff Records during the ska revival. In this way he took Jamaican music to the rest of the world, even before Marley. He died in 2006.
artiest/desmond-dekker.listen: Listen to Israelites. Notice the bouncing, angular rhythm of the rocksteady and Dekker's singing, which laments hard work and poverty yet still sounds cheerful.

artiest/desmond-dekker-en-the-aces.text:
Desmond Dekker, born Desmond Adolphus Dacres, was a Jamaican singer and songwriter regarded as a pioneer of ska, rocksteady and reggae. He was born in 1941 in Kingston and as a boy was used to singing hymns. In 1961 he auditioned for Coxsone Dodd and Duke Reid, without success, and then got a contract with Leslie Kong's label. With his backing group The Aces, consisting of Wilson James and Easton Barrington Howard, he had one of the first international reggae hits. He also spotted the talent of Bob Marley, a fellow welder, and brought him to Kong's attention.

In the early years he dealt in his songs with moral and social themes, such as respect for your parents, and later also with rude boy songs such as Rude Boy Train and Rudie Got Soul. His debut album was called 007 (Shanty Town). In 1968 Israelites appeared, which topped the British charts in April 1969 and reached the American top ten in June 1969. Dekker was the first Jamaican artist with an American hit in Jamaican style, apart from Millie Small. In 1970 he reached number two in Great Britain with You Can Get It If You Really Want, written by Jimmy Cliff. In 1975 Israelites was a British top hit again. In 1980 he signed to Stiff Records and recorded Black & Dekker, during the 2 Tone revival of ska.

Dekker brought the music of Jamaica to an international audience. His Israelites is one of the best-known examples of that breakthrough.
artiest/desmond-dekker-en-the-aces.listen: Listen to Israelites. Notice the rhythm and the singing: what makes this song different from the British and American pop singles of the time?

artiest/destiny-s-child.text:
Destiny's Child came into being in 1990 in Houston, Texas. Beyoncé Knowles and LaTavia Roberson were in a girl group that performed with rap and dance at talent shows in the city. Kelly Rowland, who was then living in Beyoncé's home, joined in 1992. Under the name Girl's Tyme they lost a national television talent contest. After that Beyoncé's father Mathew Knowles became their manager. He cut the group back to four members, with LeToya Luckett as the fourth. In 1996 they signed to Columbia as Destiny's Child.

The first hit was No, No, No. The second album, The Writing's on the Wall (1999), became their best-selling record, with the American number ones Bills, Bills, Bills and Say My Name. Behind the scenes there was friction: Roberson and Luckett felt that the manager favoured his daughter and Rowland, and in 2000 they were replaced. Michelle Williams stayed, and from then on the group was a trio. Survivor (2001) processed those conflicts and produced the hits Independent Women and Bootylicious. After a break for solo projects, Destiny Fulfilled followed in 2004, and in 2006 the group officially disbanded.

Destiny's Child was known for its tight harmonies, polished performances and lyrics about independent, strong women. The group played a major part in the return of girl groups in the 1990s and helped shape the half-sung, half-rapped vocal style of modern r&b. Destiny's Child is one of the best-selling girl groups in history.
artiest/destiny-s-child.listen: Listen to Say My Name (1999). Notice the quick, rhythmic way of singing, almost rapping, in the verses, and the shifting beat on which the three voices alternate and complement one another.

artiest/detlev-glanert.text:
Detlev Glanert is a German opera composer, born in 1960 in Hamburg, who also wrote a great deal of work for chamber and symphony orchestra, including three symphonies. He came to music late: he learned to play the trumpet at the age of eleven and only began his composition studies in his twenties, with Diether de la Motte and Günther Friedrichs, among others. He also studied for four years with Hans Werner Henze. In 1972 he saw his first operas in Hamburg, Die Zauberflöte and Die Soldaten, and from that moment he loved opera.

At Henze's invitation he wrote his first major piece of music theatre, Leyla und Medjun, for the first Munich Biennale. His breakthrough came in 1995 with the opera Der Spiegel des großen Kaisers, which received the Rolf Liebermann Prize. In 1999 the premiere of Joseph Süß followed, and in 2006 Caligula, based on the play by Albert Camus, was staged in Frankfurt. Glanert became a member of the Freie Akademie der Künste in Hamburg.

He seeks contact with the audience. Music should say something about the life of the listener, he believes. Usually he takes a familiar story and gives it a contemporary twist. In Caligula the emperor is not mad but cruel by free choice. His style emerged somewhere between Mahler and Ravel, after he had first worked for three years in Henze's shadow. He also arranged Brahms, such as the Vier ernste Gesänge.
artiest/detlev-glanert.listen: Listen to his arrangement of Brahms's Vier ernste Gesänge. Notice how a familiar work acquires a new colour with an orchestra.

artiest/deutsches-symphonie-orchester-be.text:
The Deutsches Symphonie-Orchester Berlin, DSO for short, is a German radio orchestra in Berlin. It gave its concerts mainly in the Philharmonie. It was founded in 1946 by the American occupying forces as the RIAS Symphonie-Orchester, named after the Rundfunk im amerikanischen Sektor, the broadcaster of the American sector. The first chief conductor was Ferenc Fricsay. In 1956 it received its later name.

The orchestra was led by a succession of well-known conductors. After Fricsay came Lorin Maazel from 1964 to 1975, Riccardo Chailly from 1982 to 1989, Vladimir Ashkenazy, Kent Nagano, Ingo Metzmacher, Tugan Sokhiev and Robin Ticciati. In 2026 Kazuki Yamada will follow. Between Maazel and Chailly there was no permanent chief; in those years it worked with Erich Leinsdorf, Eugen Jochum and Neville Marriner. The DSO recorded for Deutsche Grammophon, Sony Classical and Harmonia Mundi. From the 1950s date recordings of operas such as Die Zauberflöte in 1955 and Don Giovanni in 1959. In 2011 it won a Grammy for its recording of Kaija Saariaho's opera L'amour de loin, conducted by Kent Nagano.

The DSO thus began as the orchestra of an American radio station in a divided Berlin and grew into a permanent part of the city's musical life.
artiest/deutsches-symphonie-orchester-be.listen: Listen to the 1959 recording of Don Giovanni. Notice how the orchestra carries the drama: the opera begins with a heavy, menacing chord.

artiest/dewey-redman.text:
Dewey Redman was an American saxophonist who played free jazz, as a bandleader and in groups led by Ornette Coleman and Keith Jarrett. He was born in 1931 in Fort Worth, Texas, and at high school already played in the school band with Ornette Coleman, Prince Lasha and Charles Moffett. He was a cousin of the swing bandleader Don Redman. After a brief study of electrical engineering and his military service, he studied education and taught children, while playing saxophone in the evenings and at weekends. In 1959 he moved to San Francisco.

Redman played mainly tenor saxophone, sometimes also alto saxophone, clarinet and the Chinese suona, which he called a musette. His best-known period was his collaboration with Ornette Coleman from 1968 to 1972. After that he played from 1971 to 1976 in Keith Jarrett's American Quartet. Under his own name he recorded Tarik in 1970, The Ear of the Behearer in 1973 and Coincide in 1975, among others. He was also a member of Old and New Dreams, a group built around musicians from Ornette Coleman's circle. In 2001 the documentary Dewey Time was made about him. He died in 2006 in Brooklyn. His son is the saxophonist Joshua Redman.

Redman belongs to the saxophonists who carried on the free jazz of Ornette Coleman and who found a voice of their own in Keith Jarrett's group.
artiest/dewey-redman.listen: Listen to a track from Tarik or The Ear of the Behearer. Notice his tenor saxophone: what kind of tone does it have?

artiest/dexter-gordon.text: The tenor saxophonist Dexter Gordon, from Los Angeles, played in the 1940s in the bands of Lionel Hampton and Billy Eckstine. He combined the light tone of Lester Young with the language of bebop and himself became a model for Sonny Rollins and John Coltrane. After years of drug problems he made Go and A Swingin' Affair for Blue Note in 1962. After that he lived for almost fifteen years in Copenhagen, from where he played widely in Europe, including in the Netherlands. In 1976 he returned to New York. In 1986 he played the lead role in Bertrand Tavernier's film Round Midnight, which earned him an Oscar nomination.
artiest/dexter-gordon.listen: Hear the big, relaxed tone that always sits a little behind the beat.

artiest/dhani-harrison.text:
Dhani Harrison is an English-American musician, composer and singer, born in 1978 the son of George Harrison of The Beatles and Olivia Harrison. He is named after the sixth and seventh notes of the Indian scale, dha and ni, and Dhani is also a raga from North Indian classical music. He grew up in the country house Friar Park in Henley-on-Thames and studied industrial design and physics at Brown University. He first went to work as a car designer at McLaren before choosing music.

His musical career began with helping with his father's recordings. After his father's death in 2001 he completed the album Brainwashed together with Jeff Lynne; it appeared in 2002 and won a Grammy for Marwa Blues. In 2004 he stood on stage with Tom Petty, Steve Winwood, Jeff Lynne and Prince for the performance of While My Guitar Gently Weeps at his father's induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 2006 he founded the band thenewno2, which played at Coachella and Lollapalooza, among other festivals. Since 2013 he has also composed film music, together with Paul Hicks, including for Beautiful Creatures, Good Girls Revolt and Seattle Road. He toured with Eric Clapton and played several times with Pearl Jam.

His work shows how the musical legacy of a Beatle resounds in the next generation, in rock and in film music.
artiest/dhani-harrison.listen: Listen to While My Guitar Gently Weeps by The Beatles and then to a track by Dhani Harrison, for example IN///PARALLEL. What do you hear of the father in the son?

artiest/diabolus-in-musica.text:
Diabolus in Musica is a French ensemble for medieval music, founded in 1992 in Paris and based in Tours. Its leader is Antoine Guerber, who studied medieval music with Dominique Vellard at the Centre de Musique Médiévale de Paris and at the Conservatoire National Supérieur in Lyon.

The ensemble specialises in music from the Middle Ages and the early Renaissance. Its records begin in 1997 with La Chambre des Dames and Manuscrits de Tours. They cover songs of the trouvères, the polyphony of the Notre-Dame school in Paris in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, crusade songs and political songs from the years 1188 to 1250, and church music such as the Missa Magna from papal Avignon. The group also recorded work by Johannes Ockeghem, Jean Mouton and Pierre de la Rue, up to and including Reine du Ciel in 2021.

In this way the group brings a distant past back to life: the song art of the trouvères and early polyphony, long before there was any such thing as pop music.
artiest/diabolus-in-musica.listen: Listen to a trouvère song on La doce acordance. Notice how a song from the Middle Ages sounds without modern instruments.

artiest/diabolus-in-musica-en-antoine-gu.text:
Diabolus in Musica is a French ensemble for medieval music. It was founded in Paris in 1992 and is based in Tours. Its leader is Antoine Guerber, who studied medieval music with Dominique Vellard at the Centre de Musique Médiévale de Paris and at the early music department of the Conservatoire National Supérieur in Lyon. His training with Vellard places him in a French school that wants to understand medieval singing afresh, with attention to pronunciation, text and the way voices sounded together in that period.

In the course, the ensemble represents the Messe de Nostre Dame by Guillaume de Machaut, a fourteenth-century work. Machaut was a poet and composer from France, and his mass of around 1360 is regarded as one of the first polyphonic masses conceived as a whole by a single composer. The Kyrie, the opening section, lets you hear how medieval polyphony sounds: long, open chords and lines that each go their own way.

Ensembles such as Diabolus in Musica make sure that such music does not exist only on paper. They research how the notes were performed in the Middle Ages, and let us hear how strange and beautiful that sound can be to ears accustomed to pop and classical music.
artiest/diabolus-in-musica-en-antoine-gu.listen: Listen to the Kyrie of the Messe de Nostre Dame and notice how the voices sound together: the chords sound open and hollow, and the lines move independently of one another. What atmosphere does that evoke in you?

artiest/diana-ross.text:
Diana Ross was born on 26 March 1944 in Detroit. Her mother wanted to call her Diane, but Diana ended up on the birth certificate by mistake. Smokey Robinson was a boy from the neighbourhood. In 1959 she formed the group The Primettes with Mary Wilson, Florence Ballard and Barbara Martin. After signing with Motown, the group was called The Supremes from 1961.

The Supremes became Motown's most successful act of the 1960s. Almost all of their big hits were written and produced by Holland-Dozier-Holland. With twelve number ones on the US Billboard Hot 100, they are the most successful girl group in chart history. Ross left the group at the end of 1969 and began a solo career. Her first big hit was in 1970, a new version of Ain't No Mountain High Enough. After that came, among others, Touch Me in the Morning, Theme from Mahogany (Do You Know Where You're Going To), Love Hangover, Upside Down, I'm Coming Out and Endless Love. In 1973 she made a duets album with Marvin Gaye.

Ross was also an actress. For her role as Billie Holiday in Lady Sings the Blues (1972) she received a Golden Globe and an Oscar nomination. Later she appeared in Mahogany (1975) and The Wiz (1978). Her clear, somewhat restrained voice and her polished presentation fitted exactly the polished style with which Motown wanted to reach a broad audience. Between 1964 and 1981 she sang on eighteen American number ones. In 1988 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with The Supremes.
artiest/diana-ross.listen: Listen to Ain't No Mountain High Enough in the 1970 version by Diana Ross. Notice how the song builds slowly, with spoken passages and strings, before the chorus finally bursts out at full strength.

artiest/dick-dale.text:
Dick Dale was an American guitarist and a pioneer of surf music. He was born in 1937 as Richard Anthony Monsour in Boston, the son of a Lebanese father and a mother of Polish-Belarusian descent. He received the name Dick Dale in 1955 from an entertainer in the country bars where he played. He used Middle Eastern scales and plenty of reverb, which became the trademark of surf guitar. Being left-handed, he played a right-handed guitar upside down.

Let's Go Trippin' is regarded as one of the first surf rock songs. Jungle Fever and Surf Beat followed on his own label Deltone. His first album, Surfers' Choice, appeared in 1962 and was released nationally by Capitol Records. Dale appeared in films and on The Ed Sullivan Show, where he played his signature Misirlou. Together with Leo Fender he developed equipment that could sound much louder, including the first hundred-watt guitar amplifier. Because of his loud amplifiers and thick strings he was nicknamed the Father of Heavy Metal. With the British Invasion in 1964 the national popularity of surf music faded. In the 1990s he made a comeback, after Quentin Tarantino used his recording of Misirlou in Pulp Fiction.

Dale is known as the King of the Surf Guitar. He helped spread fast tremolo playing on electric guitar, and his sound influenced surf bands such as the Beach Boys and Jan and Dean.
artiest/dick-dale.listen: Listen to Misirlou. Notice the lightning-fast picking of a single string and the Middle Eastern scale.

artiest/dick-dale-en-his-del-tones.text:
Dick Dale, born Richard Anthony Monsour in 1937 in Boston, was an American rock guitarist and a pioneer of surf music. His father had Lebanese roots and his mother Polish-Belarusian. He grew up in Quincy, learned piano as a child and later bought a guitar from a friend for eight dollars. His early playing on the tarabaki, a Middle Eastern drum, shaped his guitar technique. He began in country bars and in 1955 received the name Dick Dale from an entertainer called Texas Tiny.

Dale became known as the King of the Surf Guitar, also the title of his second album. He used Middle Eastern scales, experimented with reverb and made the tremolo technique on electric guitar famous: fast, staccato picking of a single note. Together with Leo Fender he worked on new amplifiers that sounded much louder, including the first hundred-watt guitar amplifier. His version of the folk song Misirlou came out in 1962. Tarantino used the recording in Pulp Fiction, after which Dale returned in the 1990s with four albums and world tours.

Bands such as the Beach Boys, Jan and Dean and the Trashmen were influenced by Dale, and guitarists such as Jimi Hendrix, Pete Townshend, Eddie Van Halen and Brian May named him as an example. Because he sought out the limits of amplification, he is also regarded as one of the fathers of heavy metal. In 2003 Rolling Stone placed him 31st among the greatest guitarists of all time.
artiest/dick-dale-en-his-del-tones.listen: Listen to Misirlou and notice the lightning-fast repeated notes of the guitar, the reverb and the Middle Eastern scale. Can you hear how the rapid picking makes the melody sound almost like a drum?

artiest/dick-morrissey.text:
Dick Morrissey was a British jazz musician and composer, born in 1940 in Horley, Surrey. He played tenor saxophone, soprano saxophone and flute and was regarded as one of the best British jazz musicians of his time, although he also worked occasionally in rock and rhythm and blues. He taught himself to play and at sixteen began on clarinet in the school band The Delta City Jazzmen. In the 1960s he came to the fore in the wake of Tubby Hayes.

He made his name as a hard bop player, played regularly at the Marquee Club from 1960 and recorded his first solo album, It's Morrissey, Man!, in 1961. He played briefly in Ted Heath's big band. In 1966 and 1967 he came second in the Melody Maker Jazz Poll, behind Hayes. Many American musicians who toured in Great Britain recorded with him, including Brother Jack McDuff and Jimmy Witherspoon. In 1969, with the guitarist Terry Smith, he founded the early jazz rock group If. After If broke up in 1975, he toured with Alexis Korner and with the Average White Band, and met the guitarist Jim Mullen. Together they formed Morrissey-Mullen, at the time the most admired British jazz fusion band. They made seven albums in sixteen years, including After Dark in 1983.

Morrissey showed that British jazz could embrace both hard bop and jazz rock. He died in 2000.
artiest/dick-morrissey.listen: Listen to a track from After Dark by Morrissey-Mullen. Notice how the saxophone and the guitar share the melody.

artiest/dick-raaijmakers.text:
Dick Raaijmakers was a Dutch composer, theatre maker and thinker about music. He was born in 1930 in Maastricht and studied piano at the Royal Conservatoire in The Hague. From 1954 to 1960 he worked in the physics laboratory of Philips in Eindhoven, the NatLab, on electro-acoustic research. His nickname there was Dik NatLab. Read backwards, that became his stage name: Kid Baltan.

Under that name, together with Tom Dissevelt, he made some of the first electronic pop music in the world. They cut and spliced magnetic tape and had electronically generated sounds play cheerful little melodies. Their best-known record is The Fascinating World of Electronic Music from 1959, which includes Song of the Second Moon, which had already appeared separately earlier. In America the record later came out under that title. The French electronic musician Jean-Jacques Perrey called their work a source of inspiration.

After Philips, Raaijmakers worked at Utrecht University and had a studio of his own in The Hague with Jan Boerman. He helped to found STEIM and until 1995 taught electronic and contemporary music at the conservatoire in The Hague. Later he turned to music theatre, installations and essays, in which he linked visual art, film and science with music. He is regarded as a founder of Dutch electronic music. He died in 2013.
artiest/dick-raaijmakers.listen: Listen to Song of the Second Moon by Tom Dissevelt and Kid Baltan. Notice the beeping, humming sounds that imitate no existing instrument, yet play a friendly, almost childlike little tune.

artiest/dieter-bohlen.text:
Dieter Bohlen is a German songwriter, producer, singer and television personality, born in 1954 and raised in East Frisia. He began writing songs while still at school. In the late 1970s he wrote for Schlager singers at the Hamburg label Intersong. After that he produced six unsuccessful German singles for Thomas Anders, and together they formed the pop duo Modern Talking in 1984.

Modern Talking topped the German charts five times in a row, with You're My Heart, You're My Soul, You Can Win If You Want, Cheri, Cheri Lady, Brother Louie and Atlantis Is Calling (S.O.S. For Love). The duo was also successful in other European countries, in Asia and in Africa. In 1987 it broke up and Bohlen started the solo project Blue System. As a producer he wrote for others, including C. C. Catch, Chris Norman, Bonnie Tyler and Roy Black. For Chris Norman he wrote Midnight Lady in 1986, a big hit in Central Europe. For the 1989 Eurovision Song Contest he wrote Flieger for Germany and Nur ein Lied for Austria. Later he became a judge on the talent shows Deutschland sucht den Superstar and Das Supertalent.

Bohlen is above all the man behind a large part of German pop music of the 1980s, as a writer and producer for many artists at once.
artiest/dieter-bohlen.listen: Listen to Cheri, Cheri Lady. Notice the singing and how quickly the melody sticks.

artiest/dieterich-buxtehude.text:
Dieterich Buxtehude was a Danish composer and organist of the middle Baroque, whose work is typical of the North German organ school. He was born around 1637, probably in Helsingborg, which then belonged to Denmark. His father was an organist in Helsingborg and Helsingør, and Dieterich himself became an organist, first in Helsingborg and then in Helsingør. In 1668 he became organist of the Marienkirche in Lübeck, where he succeeded Franz Tunder and married his daughter Anna Margarethe. There were two organs there, a large one for services and a small one for devotional gatherings and funerals.

Buxtehude wrote both vocal and instrumental music, with more than a hundred surviving vocal works. Until the twentieth century he was regarded mainly as a keyboard composer. His church music is praised for its musical quality, not for innovation. His style was a great influence on other composers, such as Johann Sebastian Bach and George Frideric Handel. On record he appears mainly with organ works, such as the series L'oeuvre d'orgue from 1972 and 1973.

Buxtehude is regarded as one of the most important composers of the generation before Bach, and his organ music lets you hear where the Baroque organ tradition comes from.
artiest/dieterich-buxtehude.listen: Listen to one of his organ works and notice the sound of the organ: which stops do you hear, and how does the sound fill the church?

artiest/dietrich-fischer-dieskau.text:
Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau was a German lyric baritone and conductor, born in 1925 in Berlin. He was regarded as one of the most famous performers of the art song in the post-war period and is best known as a singer of the songs of Franz Schubert. He was taken prisoner in Italy in 1945 and in the prisoner-of-war camps sang songs for homesick German soldiers. In 1947 he began his career, with a last-minute substitution in Brahms's Deutsches Requiem without rehearsal. He gave his first song recital that same year in Leipzig.

From 1948 he was principal singer at the Städtische Oper Berlin, the later Deutsche Oper, where he made his debut as Posa in Verdi's Don Carlos. He collaborated early on with the sopranos Elisabeth Schwarzkopf and Irmgard Seefried and with the producer Walter Legge. His recordings of songs by Schubert and Hugo Wolf were an immediate success. He recorded Winterreise in 1955, among other works, as well as Die Zauberflöte and Tristan und Isolde. What made him special was the breadth of his repertoire: opera, song and oratorio in German, Italian or English. In a poll from 1999 he was named the second best singer of the century.

Fischer-Dieskau became a benchmark for the art song after the war, and his recordings of Schubert are still the starting point for many listeners.
artiest/dietrich-fischer-dieskau.listen: Listen to his recording of Winterreise. Notice how he colours the mood of the text with his voice.

artiest/digable-planets.text:
Digable Planets is an American hip hop trio, formed in 1987, with the rappers Ishmael Butler, known as Butterfly, Mariana Vieira, known as Ladybug Mecca, and Craig Irving, known as Doodlebug. Butler, originally from Seattle, met Irving in Philadelphia in the late 1980s. In 1989 Butler began working with Irving and Vieira. In 1992 the group signed to Pendulum Records and the whole trio moved to Brooklyn.

The debut album Reachin' (A New Refutation of Time and Space) appeared in 1993 and was certified gold by the RIAA. The second album, Blowout Comb from 1994, was according to critics a sharp break from the first: darker, less focused on hooks and more openly political, with references to the Black Panthers and communist symbolism. That same year the group took part in the compilation Stolen Moments: Red Hot + Cool, an album in aid of the fight against AIDS in the African American community. After that the group broke up.

Digable Planets is counted among jazz rap and alternative hip hop, two directions that in the early 1990s brought hip hop and jazz closer together.
artiest/digable-planets.listen: Listen to a track from Reachin'. Notice the jazzy atmosphere and how the three rappers alternate.
